<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Housing insecurity is a critical humanitarian concern in conflict-affected settings, where home destruction, repeated displacement, overcrowding, and disrupted services affect health, dignity, and recovery. In the Gaza Strip, the war that began in October 2023 has intensified housing and shelter insecurity among displaced and war-affected households. This study examined the extent, patterns, correlates, and perceived consequences of housing insecurity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A convergent mixed-methods design combined a household survey with semi-structured interviews. Quantitative data were collected from 420 households across the five governorates of the Gaza Strip within the study period (2 April−4 August 2026). Qualitative data were obtained from 34 displaced household members and 10 key informants. Differences in severe housing insecurity, measured with a study-specific six-component index, were expressed as crude prevalence ratios, while qualitative data were thematically analyzed and integrated with the quantitative findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the sampled households, 88.6% had been displaced at least once, and 33.6% of displaced households reported four or more displacement episodes. Complete home destruction was reported by 42.9% of households and severe damage by 28.3%. Current shelter conditions were frequently inadequate: 78.1% reported overcrowding, 72.6% lacked sufficient water for hygiene, 68.8% lacked privacy, and 62.6% felt unsafe. Using a six-component study-specific index, 283 of 420 households (67.4%) met the criterion for severe housing insecurity. The prevalence was higher among female-headed households (78.1% vs. 63.4%; crude prevalence ratio [PR] 1.23, 95% CI 1.08–1.40). It was also higher among households including a person with a disability or chronic illness (80.2% vs. 62.2%; PR 1.29, 1.14–1.46) and among those living in tents or informal sites (82.1% vs. 62.4%; PR 1.31, 1.16–1.49).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this sample, housing insecurity in the Gaza Strip was multidimensional, extending beyond physical shelter loss to include repeated displacement, inadequate services, protection risks, economic hardship, documentation loss, and psychosocial distress. The findings also point to two exploratory concepts, housing recovery uncertainty and documentary housing insecurity, as potentially important dimensions of housing insecurity in protracted conflict. Responses should integrate shelter, water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH), health, protection, cash, livelihoods, documentation support, and longer-term rights-based housing recovery.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Housing insecurity, displacement, and the right to adequate housing in the Gaza Strip: a mixed-methods study amid protracted conflict

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In fast-urbanizing areas, municipal solid waste collection still runs on a fixed schedule that ignores real-time bin state, wasting fleet capacity and leaving overflow-prone bins unserviced. The main problems are as much about governance as engineering: service delivery is unlinked from need, with no accountability signal; statutory segregation duties are unenforceable for want of an evidentiary base; enforcement instruments are ungraduated; and the distributional burden is invisible. Smart-bin systems presently address sensing or routing in isolation, funneling telemetry through one cloud tier whose wide-area latency is incompatible with time-critical hazard alerts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We present SWMS, a three-tier edge/fog/cloud system in which smart bins sense fill level, methane, temperature, and weight, district fog nodes evaluate thresholds and compute routes locally, and a cloud tier runs graduated compliance enforcement and an Eco-Score layer. All results are computational, not measurements of a deployment. No physical prototype was deployed, and all bin data are synthetic; the compliance and gamification layers were implemented but not validated by any user study, though the sensor error model was calibrated to real gas-sensor data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A seeded Monte Carlo model places the fog-mediated alert path at 30.9 ms against 233.1 ms for a cloud counterfactual, confirmed by two discrete-event simulations. A comparison with a proven optimal solution shows that greedy+2-opt closes to within 5.1%, matching the best tuned metaheuristic at three orders of magnitude lower compute. A service-parity comparison cuts daily collection distance by 37.9%, reproduced at 38.7% on an actual OpenStreetMap street network. Scalability to 20,000 bins follows
                      <jats:italic>O</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>1.72</jats:sup>
                      ), and fault injection raises overflow-alert
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      from 0.70 to 0.80 at 50% sensor faults.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We situate the design in the public-governance and regulatory-governance literatures and identify the obstacles a deployment faces: statutory authority, due process, administrative discretion, attribution in communal bins, distributive incidence, legitimacy, data protection, and municipal capacity. Because a non-zero sensor error rate entails a non-zero wrongful-penalty rate, we conclude that the compliance layer should first be deployed as a non-penal, evidentiary, and advisory instrument rather than a penal one.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Urban digital twins are increasingly used to support planning, policy, and urban governance, yet cities cannot be fully captured as stable digital representations. Building on existing understandings of digital twinning, this article argues for conceptualizing urban digital twinning as a continuing institutional planning practice. We distinguish the digital twin as a configured representational and analytical system from digital twinning as the broader practice connecting digital representation with interpretation, deliberation, governance, planning decisions, urban interventions, monitoring, institutional learning, and model revision across successive planning cycles. This perspective emphasizes the role of human judgment and institutional knowledge in responding to evolving urban conditions and planning uncertainty, offering a basis for more adaptive, transparent, accountable, and context-sensitive urban planning and governance.</jats:p>
title: Urban digital twins and digital twinning as a continuing planning practice

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid growth of electric vehicles (EVs) registrations requires a better understanding of how EV registrations vary across geographical areas. This study examines the geographical and temporal patterns of EV registrations across Regional Transport Office (RTO) regions in Tamil Nadu from 2022 to 2025.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Secondary data were obtained from the official Tamil Nadu EV Registration portal. Registrations of electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, and four-wheelers were analyzed using temporal trends, vehicle-category composition, RTO-level growth, registration concentration, and a separate analysis of Chennai RTO regions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Total EV registrations increased from 69,785 in 2022 to 165,818 in 2025, representing a 137.61% increase. Two-wheelers remained the dominant category, while four-wheelers recorded substantial growth. Tiruppur and Coimbatore emerged as important RTOs in 2025. The share of the top five and top ten RTOs decreased from 14.24% and 24.52% in 2022 to 11.28% and 19.90% in 2025, respectively. Chennai registrations increased from 11,663 to 17,499 during the study period.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings show a clear increase in EV registrations across Tamil Nadu, along with changes in the contribution of different RTO areas and vehicle categories. The lower shares of the top five and top ten RTO areas in 2025 compared with 2022 suggest that EV registrations were spread across a wider range of RTO areas. However, registration data only show the number of vehicles registered and do not provide information about actual vehicle use or the charging infrastructure required.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Electric vehicle growth in Tamil Nadu: beyond major urban centers

items.abstract: <jats:p>Cities depend on infrastructural lifelines that extend far beyond their territorial boundaries, yet urban resilience is often conceptualized through capacities located within cities themselves. This Perspective uses disruptions surrounding the Strait of Hormuz to reconsider how urban resilience is shaped by geographically dispersed infrastructure networks operating across multiple spatial and institutional scales. Drawing on emerging rerouting responses in the Gulf, particularly Saudi Arabia, the discussion traces how flows can be reconfigured across pipelines, Red Sea ports and overland logistics corridors when established maritime routes are constrained. We argue that such reconfiguration represents a potential mechanism of adaptation and should not itself be interpreted as evidence of resilience. Alternative pathways can provide additional options for maintaining essential flows, but they can also shift pressure, costs and dependencies toward other infrastructures, jurisdictions and chokepoints. Urban resilience should therefore account not only for capacities within cities, but also for the wider infrastructural connections through which essential urban functions are sustained and reorganized under disruption.</jats:p>
title: Urban lifelines and resilience beyond the Strait of Hormuz

items.abstract: <jats:p>Often promoted as a key to greener cities, walkability is widely praised for its sustainability, yet the extent to which it can be considered truly sustainable remains unclear. Despite its growing prominence in urban planning and policy, the true environmental, social, and economic impacts of walkability remain largely assumed rather than rigorously quantified. This perspective examines walkability through the three sustainability pillars, highlighting both its potential benefits and its overlooked trade-offs. Rather than treating walkability as an inherently sustainable solution, this perspective frames it as context-dependent, shaped by urban form, climate conditions, infrastructure design, and patterns of use. By synthesizing existing sustainability assessment tools and frameworks, including life cycle–based, social, and economic evaluation approaches, the perspective outlines pathways for more rigorous, holistic, and data-driven evaluations of walkability. Such approaches are essential for equitable, environmentally sound, and economically viable urban policies, and ensure that walkability meaningfully contributes to long-term urban sustainability.</jats:p>
title: Quantification of walkability in terms of sustainability

                    <jats:p>Electric vehicle (EV) diffusion depends not only on whether consumers recognize individual economic, performance, and environmental attributes, but also on how those evaluations are translated into an overall attitude and ultimately purchase intention. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), this study examines a bounded belief-attitude-intention mechanism in Bahrain by integrating three economic evaluations (price, perceived economic benefits, and policy incentives), three functional-performance evaluations (driving range, acceleration, and charging time sensitivity), and environmental values.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional survey produced 366 valid responses, which were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with 10,000 bootstrap resamples.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Policy incentives, acceleration, environmental values and consumer attitudes showed positive and significant direct relationships with EV purchase intention, whereas perceived economic benefits operated primarily through attitude. The mediation pattern was selective rather than universal, as attitudes provided indirect-only mediation for economic benefits, complementary partial mediation for policy incentives, acceleration, charging time sensitivity and environmental values, but not significant mediation for price or driving range. Additional robustness analyses materially clarified three apparently contradictory results. Price was negatively associated with intention in the simple model but became small and positive only after simultaneous adjustment for correlated determinants. Driving range was positively associated with intention at the simple level but lost unique significance in the full model. Charging time sensitivity was interpreted according to its reverse-coded measurement, distinguishing weaker endorsement of faster charging as an adoption inducement from any preference for longer charging durations. The significance pattern remained stable across alternative composite-score estimations, inclusive and restrictive measurement specifications, a non-owner EV subsample, demographic controls, and an independent bootstrap mediation analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study contributes by showing that attitude is a determinant-specific transmission mechanism rather than a universal mediator and by demonstrating how integrated EV adoption models can distinguish total associations from unique multivariate effects in an emerging Bahraini market. Practically, the findings highlight the importance for policy support, performance communication, charging convenience, and environmental value in encouraging EV purchase intentions in Bahrain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Beyond price and driving range: rethinking electric vehicle adoption in Bahrain through attitudinal mediation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Rapid urbanization in fragile and post-conflict cities creates complex challenges related to environmental degradation, informal settlement expansion, infrastructure limitations, weak governance systems, and unequal access to urban services. This study examined the relationships between Environmental Sustainability Planning, Social Sustainability Planning, Institutional and Governance Capacity, and Urban Outcomes in Mogadishu, Somalia. The study targeted a population of 933 individuals, including residents, NGO representatives, and CSO representatives engaged in urban development, governance, community development, and service delivery. A quantitative, descriptive, and correlational research design was adopted, and data were collected from 280 respondents using structured questionnaires. The measurement assessment demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity, with all constructs achieving acceptable internal consistency. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Relative Importance Index (RII), Pearson correlation, and multiple regression analysis. The findings revealed that Environmental Sustainability Planning, Social Sustainability Planning, and Institutional and Governance Capacity were positively and significantly associated with Urban Outcomes. Environmental Sustainability Planning demonstrated the strongest association with Urban Outcomes, followed by Social Sustainability Planning and Institutional and Governance Capacity. The study concludes that sustainable urban development in Mogadishu requires integrated approaches combining environmental management, inclusive planning, effective governance, and coordinated institutional action. The findings contribute empirical evidence from a rapidly urbanizing and institutionally fragile post-conflict city context.</jats:p>
title: Urban sustainability planning and urban outcomes in a rapidly growing city in Mogadishu, Somalia

items.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure has outpaced existing policy frameworks governing data center development. This mismatch between surging demand for digital infrastructure and local planning guidelines is widely acknowledged, although understudied. This study examines intergovernmental policy frameworks that either enable or restrict data center development. Using an exploratory design, we analyze both state economic incentive programs and local land use regulations. Results suggest a broad spectrum of governance approaches, ranging from “incentivizing” states that leverage legislative preemption to limit local zoning control, to “disincentivizing” states that enact moratoria and environmental mandates to safeguard local resources. These state-level interventions frequently override local autonomy, leaving local communities to manage grid, water, and social equity impacts. The friction surrounding data center development mirrors historical land-use debates in energy and housing infrastructure, proving that measures like buffering and screening are no longer sufficient. Addressing this governance gap demands proactive, resource-centered planning. We provide recommendations to streamline zoning regulations from multi-level governance perspectives, as well as recommendations on utility performance metrics, water-use disclosures, and transparent Community Benefit Agreements and engagements from the literature.</jats:p>
title: State and county approaches to data centers: patterns in the first generation

items.abstract: <jats:p>Reducing carbon emissions from holiday air travel—an important contributor to overall emissions in Western countries—is crucial for the transition to a post-carbon society. This article presents short-term findings from a randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in Switzerland, examining the effect of a digital nudging intervention aimed at reducing demand for holiday air travel. In 2025, 204 self-selected volunteers were randomized to control and treatment groups; 146 completed both baseline and first follow up surveys over a three-month intervention period. Rooted in the Model of Action Phases, the treatment consisted in a multi-component intervention combining app-based GenAI (GPT-3.5) and peer-generated content shared through the app and Instagram, leveraging social-norm and feedback mechanisms, in a gamified framework. Using individual fixed-effects panel models, we assess the short-term effects of the multi-component treatment on key psychological determinants and behavioral intention to reduce holiday air travel. The intention-to-treat analysis provides no evidence of average treatment effects on either psychological outcomes or flying intentions. However, higher levels of engagement with the intervention are associated with lower intentions to fly for holiday purposes, and with a smaller reduction in perceived descriptive norms around holiday flying. While these findings should be interpreted cautiously given differential attrition (39% in the treatment group vs. 18% in the control group) and the study's limited power to detect small-to-moderate effects, they suggest that sustained engagement with interventions combining GenAI and peer-to-peer content sharing via social media may have the potential to influence the psychological antecedents and stated intentions related to holiday air travel.</jats:p>
title: Toward less air travel: evidence from a multi-component field experiment combining GenAI and peer-based digital nudges
